sections.title: Objective type questions (2 parts of 1 mark, or 4 parts of ½ mark).

questions.q: True or False: (a) James Hargreaves invented a hand-powered spinning wheel (the Spinning Jenny). (b) The League of Nations was the first international organisation, set up in 1936 with its headquarters at Geneva.
questions.answer: (a) True (b) False — the League was set up in 1920.

questions.q: Match the inventor with the invention: (a) Samuel Crompton (b) John Wilkinson (c) George Stephenson (d) Michael Faraday — (i) Electric motor (ii) Spinning mule (iii) Drilling machine (iv) Locomotive engine
questions.answer: (a) – (ii) Spinning mule; (b) – (iii) Drilling machine; (c) – (iv) Locomotive engine; (d) – (i) Electric motor

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Explain the significance of the Meiji Restoration of 1868 in Japan's history.
questions.answer: (1) The Meiji Restoration began in 1868 with an era of ‘enlightened rule’ which transformed Japan from a closed feudal society to the first industrialised nation. (2) Japan framed a state led industrialisation policy. Many steel and textile factories were set up, education was popularised and Japanese students were sent to study in the West. Japan was the only country in Asia which emerged as an imperialist country. During the period between the two World Wars, Japan became a strong military power and supported Fascism.

questions.q: Why were children preferred as workers in coal mines during the 18th century? Two points.
questions.answer: (1) Children were employed because their small size helped them move better in the horizontal and narrow coal mines. (2) There was a tremendous increase in production which resulted in lower cost of goods. Much of her territories in Europe were given to Belgium and Poland. Plus, they were paid very low wages compared to older men and hence were preferred in factories.

or.answer: Imperialism is the practice of a powerful country extending its control over the political and economic life of another country by military conquest, political rule or other means, mainly to obtain raw materials, markets and places to invest capital.

questions.q: Why did Europeans want to trade with the East during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.answer: (1) These countries needed constant supply of raw materials and a ready market for selling the finished goods. The capitalists too needed new places and new industries to invest their surplus capital since these needs could not be fulfilled in their own countries or in neighboring areas. (2) This was because these countries were rich in resources but were politically and militarily weak and industrially backward. This one-sided trade was not profitable for European merchants so they started smuggling opium to China to demoralise the Chinese youth and exchange Chinese goods. Other countries of South East Asia also suffered under Imperialism. Since the war was spread over a very large part of the world for the first time, it is known as World War I.

questions.q: Explain any two objectives of the League of Nations.
questions.answer: (1) The main aims of the UNO are to maintain peace and security in the world, to prevent future war, to solve international disputes peacefully and to promote international cooperation. (2) Its main aims were to maintain peace and security in the world, prevent future war, promote international co-operation, settle international disputes peacefully and improve the conditions of labourers in member countries.

questions.q: Mention any two features of Fascism.
questions.answer: (1) They had a number of features which were common that is hostility to democracy and socialism, and the aim to establish dictatorship. Mussolini banned all political parties and introduced some reforms to get the support of the people. (2) Extreme Nationalism became a major force in the extension of Imperialism. The Boxer’s Rebellion was an organised terror against the Christian missionaries and exploitation of China after the division of China into spheres of influence. Both the Fascist and Nazi Parties glorified war and promised to their people that they would bring back the lost glory of their countries through war.

questions.q: Why did the industrialised countries choose Asia and Africa to extend their dominance?
questions.answer: This was because these countries were rich in resources but were politically and militarily weak and industrially backward. Africa also had weak political systems, a backward economy and society as well as weak armies.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Define imperialism. Mention two advantages of the growth of transport in the colonies which helped the spread of imperialism.
questions.answer: (1) This practice of extending control or rule over the political and economic life of another country is known as Imperialism. (2) Good roads, steamships, railways and canals were being built by industrialised nations in their own countries and in the colonies. Easy transportation of goods to and from the colonies made things easier for these countries. India which was an exporter of textile became a buyer of finished goods and exporter of raw materials. (3) Under this Policy, governmental control was exercised over industries and trade. Troops could also be easily sent to colonies. With the development of telegraph and telephone, messages could be sent easily.

or.q: Describe any three negative impacts of imperialism.
or.answer: (1) The indigenous industries were ruined and the natural resources ruthlessly exploited. (2) A large numbers of Africans were sold as slaves. Their policy of racial discrimination made the people lose their self respect as well as their confidence. (3) The wealth and resources were drained out from the colonies to the imperial countries. India which was an exporter of textile became a buyer of finished goods and exporter of raw materials. Besides, heavy taxation led to poverty of the masses.

questions.q: Mention any three impacts of imperialism on India.
questions.answer: (1) In India, the Europeans came as traders but became rulers. (2) India's prosperous economy and textile industry were destroyed; India became a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods. (3) It also led to the growth of political consciousness and the feeling of nationalism in It led to development in modern education and science which helped the nations to develop after they gained their independence. Besides, heavy taxation led to poverty of the masses.

questions.q: Explain any three consequences of the Second World War.
questions.answer: (1) It caused unprecedented loss of life, property and resources. The German Jews were either exterminated or sent to concentration camps. The Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki were almost wiped off when atomic bombs were dropped on them. The danger of nuclear holocaust was one of the major consequences of the war. (2) Germany was divided into four zones and Japan was put under US supervision; imperialism weakened and colonies in Asia and Africa became independent. (3) The USA and USSR emerged as superpowers, the Cold War began, and the United Nations was founded.

questions.q: Describe the rise of Germany as a rival of England before the First World War.
questions.answer: (1) She had little natural resources of her own and needed both overseas markets and sources of raw materials. In the last quarter of the 19th century, Germany had made tremendous economic and industrial progress and left England and France far behind in industrial production. (2) British naval supremacy was also challenged when Germany built the largest warship ‘Imperator’ and built the Kiel Canal connecting the North Sea and Baltic Sea endangering the English coast line. (3) Germany also built a railway line connecting Berlin with Baghdad which made it easier for Germany to send troops or suppliers to the East. But it posed a threat to British colonies there.

questions.q: Explain the system of alliances which developed in Europe before the First World War.
questions.answer: (1) In 1882, Germany, Austria and Italy signed the Triple Alliance pledging mutual military assistance against rival powers. (2) England, Russia and France signed the Triple Entente in 1907. (3) These countries competed with one another in producing deadly weapons which led to a race for armaments. Mutual hatred and suspicion disturbed the atmosphere of peace. (b) System of Alliances divided Europe into two hostile camps – Triple Alliance and Triple Entente – leading to tension and conflicts.

questions.q: Explain the making of the United Nations Organisation after the Second World War and its aims.
questions.answer: (1) They let loose a systematic campaign of terrorism and murder which the government showed little interest in curbing. The horrors of the war made the world leaders realise the need for an international organisation for peace. (2) World leaders such as British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, Soviet Leader Stalin and US President Roosevelt met at various conferences to decide about the formation of this organisation. Finally, on 24 October 1945 at a conference in San Francisco, the United Nations Charter was adopted by the members of 50 nations and the United Nations Organisation (UNO) was formed. (3) The main aims of the UNO are to maintain peace and security in the world, to prevent future war, to solve international disputes peacefully and to promote international cooperation. It also had another major objective to develop friendly relations among nations on the basis of equality and achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Describe six significant changes in society due to the Industrial Revolution.
questions.answer: (1) Now production could be done much faster and in large quantities which made things cheaper. Even the earlier devices were improved upon and developed into machines as the number of industries had increased. There was a tremendous increase in production which resulted in lower cost of goods. In India, the Europeans came as traders but became rulers. (2) Human labour was replaced with the machines and the domestic system of production came to an end. (3) People moved from villages to towns, creating an urban society. (4) The movement of coal from mines was totally dependent on muscle power – animals, men, women and children. Hence he forced the workers to work for long hours on low wages – sometimes 12 to 14 hours daily. (5) Society was divided into capitalists (bourgeoisie) and workers (proletariat); trade unions and labour laws arose. (6) Banking grew, and the need for raw materials and markets led to a race for colonies and imperialism.

or.q: Describe any six reasons for the First World War.
or.answer: (1) Most of Asia and Africa had already been divided up and possibilities of further expansion were not there. This resulted in rivalry between Russia and Austria. Japan was the only country in Asia which emerged as an imperialist country. (2) British naval supremacy was also challenged when Germany built the largest warship ‘Imperator’ and built the Kiel Canal connecting the North Sea and Baltic Sea endangering the English coast line. Germany also built a railway line connecting Berlin with Baghdad which made it easier for Germany to send troops or suppliers to the East. (3) (b) System of Alliances divided Europe into two hostile camps – Triple Alliance and Triple Entente – leading to tension and conflicts. (4) Later on Italy, Germany and other countries also joined the race. Mutual hatred and suspicion disturbed the atmosphere of peace. The propaganda which was created made it clear that if war broke out the whole of Europe would be drawn into it. (5) In 1908, Austria annexed two Slav states, Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading to hostility between Serbia and Austria. (c) The resurgence of nationalism in the Balkan States known as the Pan Slav Movement. (6) The murder of Archduke Francis Ferdinand became the immediate cause of the war. On 28 July 1914, Austria declared war on Serbia.

questions.q: Examine the consequences of the First World War.
questions.answer: (1) Millions died and property worth billions was destroyed; economies were shattered, causing unemployment and poverty. (2) The Treaty of Versailles held Germany guilty, imposed reparations, took Alsace-Lorraine and all its colonies and limited its army to 1,00,000. (3) Germain separated Hungary from Austria and Hungary was made an independent state. The Treaty of Sevres broke up the Ottoman Empire. (4) Two new states- Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia - were created out of the territories taken from the defeated powers. (5) Monarchies in Russia, Germany, Austria and Turkey ended; the USA and USSR rose and national movements in Asia and Africa grew stronger. (6) The League of Nations was set up in 1920. The harsh treaty also planted the seeds of World War II.

questions.q: How did the Policy of Appeasement and the rise of Fascism lead to the Second World War?
questions.answer: (1) Germany was humiliated by the Treaty of Versailles and wanted revenge; Italy was angry at getting no colonies. (2) The German version of Fascism is known as Nazism. He promised to reverse post-war settlements and restore German power and glory. Both the Fascist and Nazi Parties glorified war and promised to their people that they would bring back the lost glory of their countries through war. (3) Germany annexed Rhineland in 1936, Austria in 1938 and Czechoslovakia in 1938, while Italy attacked Ethiopia. (4) This resulted in rivalry between Russia and Austria. Later, the whole of Czechoslovakia was annexed. (5) But Ethiopia was taken over by Italy in 1935. (6) Being capitalist countries, they wanted to check the spread of Communism. This Appeasement Policy reached its climax when Hitler invited the Prime Ministers of Britain and France to Munich in August 1938. The Munich Pact was signed by them in 1938, allowing Germany to annex Sudetenland in the Northern part of Czechoslovakia. (7) Later on Italy, Germany and other countries also joined the race. She signed the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis with the fascist powers. United Nations Organisation was formed for peace and harmony in the world at the end of the war. (8) The scene was set for World War II when Germany attacked Poland on 1September 1939. Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939.
